# Automated PR review

An LLM reviewer runs on a PR when someone asks for it with `/review`, including on PRs from forks. Opening a PR or pushing to it never starts a review. The workflow posts each finding the review returns as an inline comment, tagged P0-P3, plus a summary comment that covers the PR description and any open questions. The summary opens with a status line: 🔴 for any open P0 or P1, 🟡 for anything else to report, 🟢 for nothing, then the head commit and the mode. Every summary also carries a design-risk rating (`low`, `medium` or `high`: whether a human must make a design or direction decision before merging), with a "Design" section (the design verdict, in nogpu and full runs). Every summary ends with "What's left for you", a ranked checklist to approve from: open P0 and P1 findings, the design decisions when the risk isn't low, questions, open P2s and skipped files, one line each with its place, at most ten before the rest fold away. P3s and latent bugs aren't decisions, so they stay out. Bugs it finds on `main`, in code the PR didn't write or worsen, go under "Latent bugs on main (not from this PR)", each with the open issue that tracks it or a suggested title for one; they never count as open findings. An inline finding stays open until a later review (every run re-checks the bot's earlier inline findings) judges it fixed, fixed in a PR stacked above, or moot; a commit that changes its lines doesn't close it, and neither does resolving its thread. A P0–P2 the author argues against with no code change is `disputed`: it stays open and goes on the summary's list for a person to decide. The status line and the approval rule count open findings the same way (`render_summary.open_findings`). Each run, including each `/review`, posts a new summary comment at the bottom of the conversation and hides the earlier ones as outdated. Light and nogpu reviews are advisory. A full review (`/review`) can approve a PR that meets a fixed rule, under [GPU review and approval](#gpu-review-and-approval); that is the only GitHub review the bot submits. Each review also sets the PR's `type/*` labels, one to three of `new-model`, `bug`, `perf`, `feature`, `refactor`, `test`, `docs` and `ci`, replacing any earlier ones; the `area/*`, `model/*` and `size/*` labels come from [`../workflows/pr-labels.yml`](../workflows/pr-labels.yml).

"Contributor" means the PR author's GitHub author association is `OWNER`, `MEMBER`, `COLLABORATOR` or `CONTRIBUTOR`: the team, plus anyone who has had a PR merged here. They can comment `/review light` on their own PR. Any other request (`/review light` on someone else's PR, or `/review` and `/review nogpu` on any PR) takes write access to this repo, which the workflow checks against the user's actual permission; a contributor without it who comments `/review` or `/review nogpu` on their own PR gets a one-line reply pointing to `/review light`. `/review` and `/review nogpu` also take a PR author with write access; on any other PR they get the same reply. `/review` also takes a head on this repository or a fork owned by someone with write access, since its live test runs the PR's code, and otherwise gets a reply pointing to `/review nogpu`. Someone with write access can run `/review light` on any PR, including a first-timer's.

| Trigger | Mode |
| --- | --- |
| Someone with write access comments exactly `/review` on a PR whose author has write access | `full`: `nogpu`, then a live test on GPUs, then approval if the rule holds (below) |
| Someone with write access comments exactly `/review nogpu` on a PR whose author has write access | `nogpu` (P0-P3 and design questions) |
| Someone with write access comments exactly `/review light` on a PR | `light` (P0-P2) |
| A contributor comments exactly `/review light` on their own PR, without the `skip-ai-review` label | `light` |
| Anyone who may start a review comments exactly `/review continue` after a review stopped part-way | continues that review in its mode, in a fresh session; a nogpu one takes write access for the commenter and the PR's author, like `/review nogpu`, and a stopped full review can't be continued: comment `/review` again |

The method in every mode is the [`pr-review`](../../.claude/skills/pr-review/SKILL.md) skill; [`review-prompt.md`](review-prompt.md) adds the bot's inputs, re-review scope and output. A run someone with write access starts has a turn cap meant only to stop a loop (`CLAUDE_REVIEW_MAX_TURNS_TEAM`, 2000, and a 5-hour timeout); a contributor's own light review keeps `CLAUDE_REVIEW_MAX_TURNS` (40).

**Re-reviews.** When the bot reviewed the PR before, the next run reviews only what changed since and loads only that: the commits since, or after a force-push, a rebase or a merge of `main` the interdiff (each file whose patch differs from its patch at that review, line numbers aside, as the PR has it now and after a marker as it was then, which is empty when a rebase moved them unchanged), plus the lines its earlier findings cite and the callers a new hunk changes the contract of. It re-checks each earlier finding at the head (fixed, fixed in a PR stacked above, still open, disputed, or moot). It reviews the whole PR again only when the last review skipped files or when GitHub won't give the diff. An earlier finding counts as open until a later review judges it fixed, fixed in a PR stacked above (which merges with it, and whose diff the workflow fetched for the review), or moot, whether or not someone resolved the thread.

To re-review after pushes, comment the same command again. The `skip-ai-review` label turns off the author's own `/review light`; a review someone with write access asks for still runs.

The action refuses actors without write access, which is most contributors on a fork. For those runs alone the workflow passes the PR author's login, and nobody else's, as the action's `allowed_non_write_users`.

A comment always runs `main`'s copy of the workflow and reads the rules from `main`, whatever the PR's base, so stacked PRs are reviewed the same way.

The bot reacts 👀 to a `/review` comment when it picks it up. A review that doesn't complete (an API error, running out of turns, a timeout, a fork that no longer exists) leaves a PR comment linking the log, never a red check, except when `main`'s scripts can't be checked out: the reporting step is one of them, so that failure is only in the run's log; a later failure updates that comment rather than adding another, and a later run that finishes rewrites it to point at its summary. A request the workflow declines exits green and never cancels a review in progress: the cases above get a one-line reply, and any other (no write access and not the author, or no API key) gets no comment. A review the API refuses because the account is out of credit gets a one-line reply saying so (and a warning in the log) instead of a "didn't complete" comment.

Running out of turns is handled in two ways. A review that finished but went past `--max-turns` (the action then reports a failure) still has its summary in the action's execution file, and the workflow posts it with a note. A review that stopped part-way posted nothing, inline comments included, since the workflow posts only what a finished review returns; it gets a "didn't complete" comment saying so, and a handoff is saved as a workflow artifact for 7 days. The handoff ([`session.py`](session.py) `handoff`) is built from the action's execution file, or after a timeout from the session transcript. Its reliable part is what the workflow recovers itself: the files it read, the changed files it never opened, and its latest messages, which usually say what it was doing. The prompt also asks the model to keep a progress note (candidate findings with their anchors, what it covered, what is left); that is best-effort, and adds the candidate findings when the model kept one (the prompt tells it a finding not in its note is lost). The notes list unverified leads, so they stay out of the PR conversation, though the artifact can be downloaded.

`/review continue` starts a fresh session with a fresh turn budget and gives it the handoff as `handoff.md`, rather than resuming the old session, which sends the whole old transcript again, probably after its prompt cache has expired: in a measured run, resuming after the cache expired cost about a quarter more than a fresh session, and while it is warm the two cost about the same. The fresh session knows only what the handoff says, so it rereads `AGENTS.md`, any skill its findings cite, and the code they anchor on, and it returns every finding that `pr-comments.json` doesn't already have. A continued run that stops too merges its handoff onto the one it started from. `/review continue` refuses, in a comment of its own that leaves the stopped review's comment as it was, if there is no saved handoff, if a later run already finished (any run that finishes marks the stopped review's comment resolved), if the PR has new commits since (ask for a new review of the current head with `/review light` or `/review`), or if a nogpu review is continued without the write access `/review nogpu` takes (both the commenter's and the author's). Only artifacts made by this workflow on `issue_comment` are used: a fork's own `pull_request` workflow can upload an artifact with any name.

| File | Role |
| --- | --- |
| [`../../AGENTS.md`](../../AGENTS.md) | **The substance.** Numbered invariants the reviewer checks and cites. Also read by contributors' own coding agents. |
| [`review-prompt.md`](review-prompt.md) | The bot's inputs, trust boundary, re-review scope and output. The method and bar are in `pr-review`. |
| [`../workflows/claude-review.yml`](../workflows/claude-review.yml) | The workflow, and the safety rules that come with running on `issue_comment`. |
| [`bot.py`](bot.py) | Every step of the preflight and review jobs that isn't an action, one function each, run as `python3 .github/review/bot.py <step>` ([`gpu_review.py`](gpu_review.py) holds the live-test job's, run the same way): a step's parameters are its `env:`, its outputs a dict, and every call to `gh` goes through one function, which [`../../test/ci/test_review_bot.py`](../../test/ci/test_review_bot.py) replaces. |
| [`render_summary.py`](render_summary.py) | The summary's fields (its `SCHEMA`), and the comment they render to. |
| [`session.py`](session.py) | Reads a run's execution file and transcripts: the usage record, and the handoff for `/review continue`. |
| [`replay.sh`](replay.sh) | Run the reviewer locally against a past PR, to tune before trusting it. |
| [`../../.claude/skills/benchmarking/SKILL.md`](../../.claude/skills/benchmarking/SKILL.md) | Benchmarking methodology. The reviewer reads it to judge performance claims; contributors follow it to produce them. |
| [`../../.claude/skills/async-worker/SKILL.md`](../../.claude/skills/async-worker/SKILL.md) | The worker's async step loop, stage by stage. The reviewer reads it before judging any worker-loop change. |
| [`../../.claude/skills/add-mstar-model/SKILL.md`](../../.claude/skills/add-mstar-model/SKILL.md) | The model-porting workflow end to end, plus a registration checklist and a topology map. |

Most tuning belongs in `AGENTS.md`, not in the prompt. The prompt says *how to review*; the invariants say *what is true about this codebase*, which is the part that makes the review worth more than a generic bot.

Procedural knowledge — how to run a benchmark, how to debug a hang — belongs in `.claude/skills/`, not in `AGENTS.md`. `AGENTS.md` states invariants the reviewer cites by number; a skill is a runbook an agent loads when it has that task in hand. Mirror a skill to `.agents/skills/` if you want non-Claude tooling to pick it up too.

## One-time setup

**Before merge.** Only what the workflows don't do themselves; they make the rest (the status issue, the `skip-ai-review` and `type/*` labels, the ssh key's registration with Eras) and every limit has a default.

1. **The `review-bot` environment** (Settings → Environments), with deployment branches limited to the default branch so a workflow pushed on any branch can't read it (`issue_comment` runs on the default branch, so the jobs that hold the keys pass the rule). Do this first, before adding any secret: a workflow naming an environment that doesn't exist creates it with no rule. Its secrets: `REVIEW_APP_PRIVATE_KEY`, the private key of the app in item 2; `REVIEW_SSH_KEY`, the one private key the live test reaches boxes with, kept on the runner and never sent to a box; `ERAS_API_KEY`, from an organization or wallet used only by CI with automatic top-up off; `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, the review's key, read by the preflight, review, live-test and weekly improve jobs, all of which run in this environment; and `LIVE_TEST_ANTHROPIC_KEY`, the box's Anthropic key, a key of its own since the box runs PR code with a shell: the box gets it as the Eras secret in item 4, and the job holds it only to strip its value from what the box writes.
2. **The `mstar-review` GitHub App**, owned by `mstar-project` and installed on this repository, with repository permissions Contents: read and write, Issues: write, Pull requests: write and Variables: read. Contents needs write because GitHub counts an approval only from an account that can push: on a test repository, the app's approval with Contents: read posted but didn't count (`reviewDecision` stayed `REVIEW_REQUIRED`; GraphQL's `authorCanPushToRepository` was false). An approval with write counting hasn't been seen yet, so confirm that first, on a test repository. Only the approval step's token asks for write (it runs no model and no PR code); every other token on this repository asks for read. But write lets the app's private key push to any branch `main`'s protection doesn't cover, other people's PR branches included, and make tags and releases; the key is only in the `review-bot` environment (item 1). Put its client ID in the repository variable `REVIEW_APP_CLIENT_ID`.
3. **`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`** in that environment, from the workspace in item 5. An environment secret wins over a repository or organization one of the same name, so delete any older one.
4. **`ERAS_RUN_SECRET_ID`**: save the box's Anthropic key (`LIVE_TEST_ANTHROPIC_KEY`'s value) as an Eras secret and put its id in this repository variable.
5. **Both Anthropic keys in one Anthropic workspace with a spend limit.** The bot has no cap of its own.

**Also before merge:** turn on "Require review from Code Owners" in `main`'s branch protection. `.github/CODEOWNERS` names who must approve a change under `.github/` or `.claude/` or to `.mcp.json` or `.claude.json` (the jobs that hold the keys import `.claude/`'s scripts and load its settings and MCP config), so a pushed workflow or skill can't reach the `review-bot` environment's keys on a bot approval alone (bot approvals don't count for code owners, and pushes don't dismiss them).

**At merge, in this order** (nothing checks this order, so it is the only thing keeping it):

1. Merge this PR. Doing step 2 first would block every other PR: `main` doesn't have this workflow yet, so a merge group would never report the check, and the queue would wait out its timeout and drop the entry.
2. Add `review-bot-approval-current` ([`../workflows/review-approval-current.yml`](../workflows/review-approval-current.yml)) to `main`'s required status checks, with the merge queue on and "Only merge non-failing pull requests" left on. The name to require is the job's, and its source must be pinned to GitHub Actions, or a commit status of the same name could stand in for it. On a pull request it passes at once, since a required check must report there too; in the merge queue it passes only if a person's latest review stands APPROVED, or the bot's latest approval is on the PR's current head, and any read error fails it. It runs `main`'s script with a read-only token, no model and no PR code. Pushes still don't dismiss the bot's review, so without this check, an approval from before a push could carry a merge.
3. `gh variable set REVIEW_APPROVALS --body on`. Only after step 2: nothing checks that the check is required before the bot approves.

**Optional**, none of it needed for the above to work:

- **Limits:** `REVIEW_GPU_MAX_GPUS` (4), `REVIEW_GPU_HOURS` (4), `REVIEW_GPU_MAX_USD_PER_HOUR` (30), and `REVIEW_GPU_MAX_RUNS` (2), the most live tests the bot runs at once across all PRs: `gpu.py launch` checks it (`budget.max_running`) against the live `live-pr-*` instances in the Eras organization (another reason that organization is the bot's alone). A cache refresh's boxes (the warm caches below) count toward it too, though the refresh itself starts past it.
- **Media:** a public repository under the same owner with GitHub Pages on, named in `REVIEW_MEDIA_REPO` (the name only), with the `mstar-review` app installed there (item 2's Contents: write covers the pushes). The token minted for that repository asks for write on it alone.
- **Warm caches on Eras:** Eras volumes of up to 1 TiB each for weights and compile caches, their ids space-separated in `ERAS_CACHE_VOLUMES`. An Eras box binds one volume, so they are replicas, one per box: a live test mounts the first one no box holds, read-only at `/cache`, and starts cold when every one is held. Fill or refresh them with the **Review bot cache** workflow ([`../workflows/review-cache.yml`](../workflows/review-cache.yml), run by hand), which runs only `main` and gives each volume a box of its own, two at a time, with the volume read-write: it starts each model's server once, so its kernels compile (`/cache/live-pr-compile-cache`, saved every 5 models). A refresh starts from an empty compile directory, so its first save, at model 5, replaces the volume's tarball: one cut short before that leaves the old tarball, and one cut short after it keeps only what it had finished at its last save, which can be fewer kernels than the volume held before; run it again. The job fails unless the box reached the end with its volume mounted. By default it warms only the most-used models; `all` is opt-in. By default too the weights download to the box's own disk and only the compile caches reach the volume: measured on one model, a warm start took 543 s against 704 s cold, thanks to the compile caches; weights on the volume didn't help (a volume can take a long time to hydrate on a new node: about 50 minutes, seen once, longer than downloading from the Hub). The `weights` input keeps the weights on the volumes too (`/cache/hf`). Like all Eras spend, this workflow's box time is bounded by the Eras wallet.

**A missing setting.** Without `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` the job logs a warning and exits green. Without the Eras settings a `/review` reviews and then reports that no GPUs are configured; without `REVIEW_SSH_KEY` the live test can reach none, and without `ERAS_RUN_SECRET_ID` it starts no box (it never falls back to `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`).

**The app's token.** This workflow posts with the app's token, and with the job's own token as `github-actions[bot]` until `REVIEW_APP_CLIENT_ID` and the key are both set. An app token lasts an hour, so the workflow mints a fresh one before each group of posts: the inline comments, the summary, the live-test comment and the approval all come from the app. Once `REVIEW_APP_CLIENT_ID` is set, only the app's login counts as the bot for the summaries, state and markers later runs read, since any workflow can post as `github-actions[bot]`; a forged inline comment can only add a finding, so those still count from either login. So once it is set, a summary a run posts after falling back to the job's token (the key is broken or missing) isn't read as the bot's: `/review continue` and later re-reviews don't see it. Fix the key rather than leave the fallback running. Without Variables: read or Contents: write the approval's own mint fails, so approvals stay off. A fork testing with its own app has a different login, so it must leave `REVIEW_APP_CLIENT_ID` unset.

## GPU review and approval

Anyone with write access, the author included, can start a full review (`/review`); it takes no second person and no allowlist. The PR's author must have write access too, since the live test runs the PR's code, and its head must be on this repository or a fork owned by someone with write access (an author can open a PR from anyone's fork).

A full review runs in two jobs, split by what each may hold:

- **`review`** (as for `/review nogpu`, no shell) also decides, from what the change can affect, whether and what the live test runs, and says why: `full` (the whole change), `targeted` (only what the change since the last passing live test, or the whole PR without one, reaches) or `none` (nothing in the change needs a GPU run); which kinds of check, `correctness` (served output, parity, regressions), `performance` (throughput and latency A/Bs) or both; and how many GPUs its largest config needs. Like every re-review, it starts over only from a review that skipped files. Nothing runs while the review left an open P0–P2 finding (counted as the approval rule counts them) or a skipped file: the live-test comment lists what to fix first and asks for `/review` again (an open question and the design risk don't hold the live test back, though both still stop approval). Otherwise the workflow honours the choice on every run but two cases: when the bot's last live test on the PR didn't pass on an ancestor of the head (it failed, was partial or unavailable, or ran on a commit since rebased away), the live test runs in full, with both kinds of check, whatever the review asked for, so a failure is never hidden; and so does a re-review's `targeted` when no live test ran before it, since no GPU run covered the commits that review built on, and its `none` too unless the PR touches no runtime code. A re-review with `untestable` set is exempt from both: that PR can't be approved, so a full run would rent GPUs for nothing. After a pass on an ancestor, a `targeted` run is told that commit and gets that test's report, as data. A `none` that stands starts no box: the PR's comment says "No GPU run: " and the review's reason.
- **`live-test`** runs no model and no PR code. [`gpu_review.py`](gpu_review.py) gets GPUs through `live-pr-test`'s [`gpu.py`](../../.claude/skills/live-pr-test/scripts/gpu.py): the cheapest open Eras listing under the hourly cap. It starts [`gpu_review_box.sh`](gpu_review_box.sh) there as the job itself: one Claude Code session that follows `live-pr-test` against the reviewed commit and writes a report, media and a verdict. Before any server starts, it runs CI's tests with the GPUs visible, so the CUDA tests GitHub's CPU job skips run too; a test only the PR fails makes the verdict Fail. The job waits, copies them back, posts the report (images inline, audio and video in a gallery), and decides approval.
- **When there are no GPUs**, it posts what it found (Eras listings and prices) and stops; the review stands without approval.
- **The box** gets the PR's public code, a fixed brief, the review's notes and the PR's title and description as data (`findings.json`, `pr-body.md`) and its own spend-capped Anthropic key, never a GitHub token, the ssh key or the Eras key. It ends when its session does, and the Eras Pod's deadline ends it anyway, whatever happens to the workflow.
- **Media** go to a separate repository served by GitHub Pages (`REVIEW_MEDIA_REPO`), not into this one, whose every clone would carry them: audio, images and video only (never a page or script), up to 100 MB a run, and the newest runs that fit in 900 MB (Pages serves at most 1 GB), kept as a single commit. The comment links the gallery only once the push succeeded. The report and result kept as the run's artifact are the redacted copies.

**The approval rule** (`gpu_review.py approve`), all of: the review finished on its own; the PR's head is still the reviewed commit; the author has write access and the head repository is this one or owned by someone with write access; the live test passed on that commit, or the review chose `none` and it stood (the last live test passed on an ancestor, or there is none and the review didn't build on an earlier one or the change touches no runtime code, as above), and either that live test exists or the change touches no runtime code (only files the labels put in `area/docs`, `area/tests` or `area/benchmark`), so a model's word alone never approves code no GPU ran (the approval then says the review found nothing that needs a GPU run); the review rated the design risk `low` (the PR follows the existing design and decides nothing the team hasn't: no new abstraction, shared-layer restructuring or public surface, and no change to security-relevant code: credentials, auth, API keys and secrets handling, redaction, and the bot's own workflows and sandbox, not every path a request takes) with no open question and no skipped file; no open P0–P2 finding, however its thread was closed (a thread of the bot's that someone edited counts as an open P0; a re-review's `fixed` or `moot` on a bot thread none of whose lines changed counts as `disputed`, so the checklist names it and says why, and a person decides or changes one of those lines, and so does one on an earlier finding outside the diff, which has no thread, unless the commits since the last review touched its file, where not knowing counts as untouched; and an inline finding this run posted that has since been deleted or retagged stops the live test and the approval); and the change touches none of the bot's own rules, CI, or the dependencies and toolchains (`.github/`, `scripts/`, `docker/`, `tools/`, `packaging/`, `.claude/`, `.cargo/` or `.husky/` at any depth, `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `CLAUDE.local.md`, `MANIFEST.in`, `pyproject.toml`, `setup.py`, `setup.cfg`, `uv.toml`, `.mcp.json`, `.claude.json`, `.ripgreprc`, any `Cargo.toml`, `rust-toolchain`, `rust-toolchain.toml` or `requirements*.txt`, any lockfile, `.gitmodules` and any submodule, compared against the default branch so retargeting the PR can't hide a file). A stacked PR is judged on two file lists: this rule, its runtime-code check included, counts files against the default branch, so it sees the PRs below too, and the checklist says so, while a re-review's `none` is overruled by the PR's own files against its base (`touches_runtime`), as above. Other areas are left to the findings, the live test and the design-risk rating. A PR with anything the live test can't exercise (the review's `untestable` field: hardware the bot's GPUs aren't, more GPUs or nodes than a run gets, weights or services it can't get; a review asking for more GPUs than `REVIEW_GPU_MAX_GPUS`, which the workflow adds to that field; or the PR's title, file names or changed lines matching `UNTESTABLE_HARDWARE` in `gpu_review.py`, which catches what a word can) is reviewed as usual but never approved: it goes on "What's left for you" naming what the live test can't cover, and a diff that can't be read counts the same. The bot then approves that commit. A later push doesn't dismiss the approval: it stays on the PR, attached to the commit it covers, which its text names, but it no longer counts for a merge: the required check `review-bot-approval-current` passes in the merge queue only when a person's approval stands (as `main`'s protection already requires of one), or the bot's latest approval is on the PR's current head. After a push, a merge needs a new `/review` or a person's approval. Otherwise the live-test comment lists the conditions that failed in its "What's left for you" checklist, with the review's own open items; a human approves from that list.

**The kill switch.** Approvals happen only when the repository variable `REVIEW_APPROVALS` is `on`, read through the API right before the bot would approve, so a live test that started hours ago still obeys it. Unset, any other value or a failed read means off: reviews and live tests run and post as before, no GitHub review is submitted, and the comment says what the rule would have done. Turn approvals off at once with `gh variable set REVIEW_APPROVALS --body off`; approvals already posted stay.

A live test with a 👂 row (media only a human can judge) is `partial`, so it is never approved, and the next `/review` runs the live test in full.

Under `main`'s current classic protection (1 required approval) the bot's approval counts as that one review: an author with write access can comment `/review` on their own PR and, if the rule holds, merge with no person having looked. No classic setting stops an app's approval from counting; to require a person as well, raise required approvals to 2.

## Tuning loop

Do this before anyone comes to rely on it. The failure mode for a review bot is not missing a bug — it is being noisy enough that contributors stop reading it, after which it catches nothing at all.

```bash
.github/review/replay.sh 295        # a PR where review caught something real
.github/review/replay.sh 328        # a large, mostly-mechanical PR
```

Pick ten or so merged PRs: a few where a human reviewer caught a genuine defect, a few that were clean, and a couple of big refactors. Then:

- **Missed a real defect** → the invariant it should have cited is missing or too vague in `AGENTS.md`. Add it with the concrete failure mode, not as a principle.
- **Reported something nobody would ask for a change on** → tighten the "Don't report" list in `pr-review` §2. Being specific about the *category* works better than lowering a severity dial.
- **Rambled or padded to look useful** → the bar in `pr-review` §2 is the lever: every finding that meets it, and none that don't.

Track hit rate across the sample as you change things; it is easy to fix one case and regress two.

## Promoting it to a required check

Reasonable criteria, once you have replay data:

- Over your last ~20 PRs, at least 80% of its findings are ones a maintainer agrees with.
- It has caught at least one defect that human review missed.
- Median runtime under ten minutes, and it does not flake.

Even then, prefer not making it a required check: a non-deterministic check shouldn't have veto power over a merge. The bot's approvals after a full review are a separate thing, governed by the approval rule.

## Cost control

Current levers, roughly in order of effect: nothing runs automatically, only on request with a `/review` command, which takes write access or authorship of the PR (`/review light` only for authors, and `skip-ai-review` stops them), and for `/review` and `/review nogpu` an author with write access too; `concurrency` cancels a run superseded by a newer one on the same PR; a contributor's own light review triages a diff over about 4,000 lines rather than covering it in full, and `--max-turns 40` caps it (`/review continue` grants another 40; the `CLAUDE_REVIEW_MAX_TURNS` repository variable overrides it); a run someone with write access starts reviews a big diff in slices with subagents, with a cap meant only to stop a loop (`CLAUDE_REVIEW_MAX_TURNS_TEAM`, 2000) and a 5-hour timeout. A full review adds GPU time, bounded by the Eras wallet and the limits under [One-time setup](#one-time-setup). The model is pinned to Opus in the workflow, at effort `high` in every mode (Claude Code's default without `--effort` is medium); lowering it to `medium` is the next cost lever. Drop to Sonnet if cost matters more than recall and replay shows it catching the same defects.

**Monitoring.** A daily job ([`../workflows/review-monitor.yml`](../workflows/review-monitor.yml), no model) writes the **status issue** (`Review bot status`, which its first run creates; subscribe to it; it is bot-owned and found by a hidden marker, so don't create it by hand). The issue's body lists whether approvals are on and every PR merged in the last 60 days with the bot's approval (GitHub's own record, so the bot keeps none), with what later happened to it (a revert on `main`, a cross-reference that reports or fixes a bug, a later fix that changed its lines by `git blame`, a CI check that failed on the merge commit but passed on its parent). New signals go out as one comment, so subscribers get at most one notification a day. It changes nothing else and adds nothing to the merge queue.

**What to improve.** Once a week a job ([`../workflows/review-improve.yml`](../workflows/review-improve.yml)) opens one issue, "Review bot: what to improve, week of <date>", with a ranked list of changes to the bot's skill or code, each with its evidence and where to make it. It gives a model with the review's restrictions and no web the past 7 days of evidence (the bot's summaries and findings and the replies to them, findings judged moot, findings resolved with their lines unchanged, what people raised that the bot didn't, the monitor's signals, stopped reviews, failed or unavailable GPU runs), with logins removed and comments clipped; all of it is untrusted data. A week with nothing worth raising opens no issue. It runs once a week. It never edits code, opens a PR or changes the bot.

Every run that reaches Claude records what it used: API calls (one per API response in the transcript, however many lines it spans), uncached input, cache-write, cache-read and output tokens (per model from the run's result, which also counts calls the transcript doesn't hold, or summed from the transcript when a timeout leaves no result), turns and cost (priced from the tokens at list prices when a timeout leaves no cost), with the mode, whether it was a `/review continue`, the PR and the head commit. It goes in the run's job summary as a table, never on the PR. The GPU box's own Claude session isn't in that table: the job that waits for the box prints the cost the box reports (its `claude.json`, which the PR's code could have written) to the job's log.

**The limit.** The bot keeps no record of what it spends and enforces no cap of its own. Claude spend is bounded by the Anthropic workspace's spend limit; GPU time is bounded by the Eras wallet and the limits under [One-time setup](#one-time-setup).

## Threat model

`issue_comment` runs with secrets on PRs from forks, so the PR's contents and comments are untrusted input. A comment only selects the mode, by exact match in the workflow's expressions (the preflight job's `if` and its command, one of a few fixed words); its text never reaches a shell or the prompt. The workflow never executes PR code, checks the PR out only into `pr-head/`, reads its rules from the base tree, gives the model no shell and no mutation tools (it returns its inline comments and summary as fields, and a step that runs no model posts them), confines its reads to the checkout (the base tree and `pr-head/`, every file of which it may read), redacts credential-shaped strings and the job's own token (as is and base64) from everything it posts, makes mentions, links and images in model text inert, makes the model and box text in its summary and live-test comments inert (`render_summary.inert`: no pings, links or images, apart from fenced code, which GitHub shows as written, and a report's bare `<details>` and `<summary>` tags; the inline comments too, which the model returns as fields and a step that runs no model posts), and holds write permission on pull requests and issues of this repository (and, in full mode, contents of the media repository, and contents of this repository for the approval step alone, which runs no model and no PR code: GitHub counts an approval only from an app that can push). Those are what each token asks for; the app's private key (`REVIEW_APP_PRIVATE_KEY`) can mint a token with everything the app was granted, contents write on this repository included (a push to any branch `main`'s protection doesn't cover, other people's PR branches too, and tags and releases), so it is a secret to guard like the API key, and it is only in the `review-bot` environment. The review can fetch pages only from the sites the workflow lists and Claude Code's built-in documentation sites, and it can run `WebSearch`, which has no domain list; it has no shell, and its reads are confined to the checkout with `.git` denied, because the action writes this job's token into the root checkout's `.git/config` (`Read` deny rules, which also cover `Grep`, `Glob` and a symlink a PR plants in `pr-head/`). So a fetch has no secret to carry out, as long as those rules hold; fetched content is untrusted input like the PR. In light and nogpu mode the residual risk is a misleading comment. In full mode a misleading review can also feed the approval rule, which the next paragraph bounds.

A full review adds one place PR code runs: the GPU box, and only for a PR whose author has write access (checked against their permission, not their association) and whose head is on this repository or a fork owned by someone with write access. The privilege split keeps the rest as above: the `live-test` job holds the ssh and Eras keys and the app token but runs no model and no PR code; the box runs the model with a shell and the PR's code but holds none of those. The box's session reads skills from `main`'s tree and has the Skill tool off. Its brief is fixed text plus the commits, the review's `full`/`targeted` call and its kinds of check (only those words: `gpu_review.py` reads them from the review and checks them again at start), and, when the workflow made the run full, which call the review made and a fixed reason; the review's model-written notes and the PR's description go beside it as `findings.json` and `pr-body.md`, which the brief calls untrusted data, so text an attacker gets into the review reaches the session only as data, never as its instructions. To keep a stranger's text further from that session, in full mode the review reads only the comments and issue titles of the team (`OWNER`, `MEMBER`, `COLLABORATOR`) and the bot's own comments. What the box can reach is still wide, and that is the residual risk. Its Anthropic key is in the environment of every process there, the PR's code included, so it is a key of its own (`LIVE_TEST_ANTHROPIC_KEY`, spend-capped, never the review's key). The session and the PR's code run as root in an Eras Pod of their own, and reach whatever its network reaches; the session gets a fresh home and Claude config, so it loads no settings or hooks the image came with. What the box writes is posted only after redaction of the credential patterns and the exact values of every secret the job holds. A live-test pass shows the PR didn't break by mistake; it can't show a hostile author is honest, since the PR's code runs on the box as the same user and can write `result.json`. The approval is a fixed rule over the review's fields, the live test's verdict and the file list, so a misleading review can't approve a change to the review rules or dependencies. Text that gets a review to choose `none` skips the GPU run, but that approves only a change to docs, tests or benchmarks, or the commits since a passing live test, and every other condition still holds. A contributor's run on their own PR reads exactly the content a maintainer's review of that PR would, with the same tools and token, so it adds cost exposure (bounded by the rules above and one run at a time per PR), not new capability. The live-test history and the saved review state (each summary's findings and outside-the-diff items) that the workflow reads are the bot's own comments on the PR, which anyone with write access can edit as well as delete: rewriting a failed verdict as a pass, removing a failed one, or dropping a finding from the saved state lets the next run build on a pass or a state that never happened, or on none, so this too rests on trusting write access, as running the PR's code does. The bot's inline findings are an exception only for edits: an edit shows up on the thread, so it is caught (see the approval rule), and so is deleting one this run posted before this run's approval. Deleting one before the next review isn't caught: that review no longer sees it. A saved handoff (for `/review continue`) is a public artifact holding the model's notes on the PR's content, redacted like everything else the bot posts; a continued run trusts only artifacts from this workflow's own `issue_comment` runs, checks the handoff's PR, head commit and mode, and gives the model its notes as untrusted input. Preserve the rules listed in the workflow header when editing it.
